title: Every WW2 Cartridge Explained — Nation by Nation
fullText: In 1943, with their cities burning and the war already slipping away, German engineers chambered a stubby little rifle round barely longer than your thumb. Almost an afterthought. It also became the ancestor of nearly every assault rifle on Earth today. The AK-47, the M16, the rifle in every war you've seen on the news. World War II wasn't only fought with tanks and bombers. It was fought with ammunition, dozens of rival cartridges, some deadly, some laughably weak, some still killing people 80 years later. Nation by nation, this is the story of the bullets that fought the deadliest war in history, Italy. The rifle round that got an American president killed didn't come from a superpower. It came from Italy. The 6.5x52 Carano was adopted back in 1891 as the standard round for the Carano Model 91 rifle and it was still soldiering on when Italy marched into World War II. Then on November 22nd, 1963, a man named Lee Harvey Oswald fired a war surplus Italian Carcano carbine in that exact caliber and killed John F. Kennedy, a World War II era boltaction he bought mail order for less than $20. One of the most infamous shots of the 20th century was fired from a plain Italian infantry rifle nobody had thought about in decades. The round itself was a strange one, a long, skinny 6.5 mm bullet with gentle recoil but weak stopping power. Italian troops grumbled that it drilled neat little holes clean through a man without knocking him down. So Italy tried to fix it, switching to a punchier 7.35x51 cartridge right before the war. Then couldn't build enough of the new ammo or the new rifles to match. The result? Italian soldiers ended up juggling two different rifle calibers across the North African desert. A supply line nightmare in the worst possible place to have one. Their pistol round was almost a joke. The 9mm Gacenti looked nearly identical to the German 9mm Parabellum, but it was loaded far weaker. Drop a real full power parabellum round into a Genti pistol and you could crack the gun apart in your hand. A cartridge pretending to be something stronger than it was. Honestly, a pretty fitting symbol for Italy's entire war. But if Italy's ammo was underpowered, the next nation built rounds designed to be almost impossible to see coming. Japan. Japanese riflemen had a quiet advantage. Half the time you couldn't tell where the shots were coming from. The 6.5x50 Arisaka feeding the Type 38 rifle was deliberately lowowered. And that turned out to be a feature, not a bug. It produced very little muzzle flash and almost no smoke. In the green hell of Guadal Canal in 1942, US Marines described firing blind at snipers they simply could not locate. No flash, no telltale smoke cloud, just men dropping around them. The recoil was so soft that shooters barely came off target between shots. But the Japanese high command decided the little 6.5 hit too softly at long range and out of machine guns. So midwar they introduced a bigger round, the 7.7x 58 Arasaka built around the type 99 rifle. And just like Italy, Japan now found itself fighting a world war with two incompatible rifle cartridges. A brutal logistics problem for an island empire trying to supply troops scattered across thousands of miles of ocean. Then there was the pistol. The 8x22 Namboo fired from the type 14. The Papa Namboo was one of the feeblest service pistol rounds of the entire war. Weaker than a modern 380, prone to jamming, more likely to annoy an enemy than stop one. Officers carried it as a badge of rank more than a real weapon. One last detail people miss. Every Arasaka rifle wore the emperor's chrysanthemum stamped into the steel, and Japanese armorers often ground it off before surrendering so the sacred symbol wouldn't fall into enemy hands. across the world. Meanwhile, the British were feeding a rifle so fast that the Germans once swore they were facing machine guns. Britain in 1914, advancing German infantry reported walking straight into machine gun fire. There were no machine guns. It was British riflemen. The cartridge behind that legend was the 303 British, adopted way back in 1889 and carried straight through both World Wars in the iconic Lee Enfield. A rifle so smooth and fast that a trained soldier could squeeze off 15 or more aimed shots a minute. They called it the Mad Minute. That's roughly double the rate of most enemy bolt actions. The 303 was a rimmed cartridge. Its base flared out like the edge of a coin, a holdover from an older age of ammunition. It made the rounds awkward to stack. Load them wrong and they'd rimlock and jam. But the Lee Enfield's designers tamed the quirk and the round went everywhere Britain fought. The freezing North Atlantic, the North African sand, the Burmese jungle. It fed the Bren light machine gun and the water cooled vicers. And early in the war, it even armed the Spitfire and Hurricane, whose wings were packed with 303 machine guns, hosing down German bombers over London. Here's a fun argument for you. The 303 entered service in 1889, just a hair before Russia's famous rifle round, so gun historians still bicker over which one is truly the oldest. Britain also fired the enemy's own pistol round right back at them. The 9 by19 Parabellum stuffed into the crude stamped metal Sten gun that cost only a few dollars to build and was air dropped to resistance fighters by the crate. And then there was the giant, the 0.55 boys, an enormous rifle round for the boy anti-tank rifle with recoil savage enough to bruise shoulders and rattle teeth. Soldiers called it the elephant gun. By 1940, it was already bouncing harmlessly off German armor, obsolete almost the day it arrived. If you didn't know, a single bullet could get a president killed or fool an entire army into hearing machine guns, do me a favor and hit subscribe. It genuinely helps the channel because the next three nations built the rounds that still decide wars right now. the Soviet Union. One of these rounds is over 130 years old and it's still killing people this week. The 7.62x 54R was designed in 1891 for the Mosen Nagant rifle and by every rule it should have been retired generations ago. It's rimmed and old-fashioned just like the British 303. Instead, it refused to die. From the Mosen Nagant to the semi-automatic SVT40 of World War II to today's PKM machine guns and Dragunov sniper rifles, it became the longest serving combat cartridge on the planet. Still in frontline use in Ukraine as you watch this more than 130 years after it was born. The Soviets built millions of Mosins around it. Crude, brutal, dead simple. It fired when caked in mud and frozen at 40 below on the eastern front. Exactly when fancier weapons choked and died. The deadliest sniper who ever lived, Finland Simo Heiha, racked up hundreds of kills in the snow with a Mosen firing this exact round. No scope, just iron sights and inhuman patience. Their submachine gun round was the opposite animal, fast and vicious. The 7.62x 62x 25 Tokarev was a hot little bottlenecked cartridge that fed the TT33 pistol and the legendary PPS-41, the Burp gun, with a 71 round drum that could empty at around 900 rounds a minute. At Stalenrad, whole Soviet squads carrying PPH drums simply drowned German attackers in a wall of close-range lead in the rubble. And then the beast, the 14.5x114, built for the PTRD and PTRS anti-tank rifles. A round as long as your hand and by midw already too slow to crack the front of a modern tank. But it survived anyway. That same cartridge still roars out of the KPV heavy machine gun today. Yet another Soviet round that outlived the country that made it. But the one most Americans actually grew up hearing about. That's next. The United States. You already know this one by its sound. A single metallic ping that legend says got men killed. It came from the M1 Garand, the first standardisssue semi-automatic battle rifle any nation fielded in force, chambered in the full power 306 Springfield. When a GI fired his last shot, the Garand kicked out its empty eight round clip with a distinct ringing ping. And the story goes that German and Japanese soldiers learned to listen for it to catch him reloading. Historians still argue over whether that ever really happened in the deafening roar of a firefight. The round didn't care. The 306 was a hammer, flat shooting, and hard-hitting, feeding the Garand, the bar, and the M1919 machine gun from the beaches of Normandy to the black sand of Euima. General Patton called the Garand the greatest battle implement ever devised, and the round is what made it hit. Not everyone needed that much rifle, though. Officers, radiomen, and truck drivers got the 30 carbine, a light, handy little round, punchier than a pistol, but a fraction of the weight of the Garands, fired from the slick M1 carbine. Up close, America swore by the 45 auto, a big, slow, heavy slug thrown by the Colt 1911 pistol, and the Thompson Tommy gun. The US had chosen it decades earlier after finding smaller rounds sometimes failed to stop a charging enemy cold. They wanted a bullet that landed like a swung sledgehammer. And then there's the monster, the 50 BMG, a cartridge nearly 5 in long, designed by John Browning at the tail end of World War I and fired from the M2 Medus. In World War II, it ripped apart aircraft, trucks, and light armor with equal ease. But here's the incredible part. It never left. More than 100 years later, that same World War II era round holds some of the longest confirmed sniper kills in history, reaching out past 2 miles. And yet, the single cartridge that changed guns forever came from the nation that was losing the war. Germany. Germany lost the war, but one of its bullets won the future. Start with the backbone. The 7.92x57 Mouser, the round of the bolt-action car, 98K, and of the most terrifying sound on the whole battlefield. Fed into the MG42 machine gun, it screamed out at around 1,200 rounds a minute, so fast the human ear couldn't separate the individual shots. It came out as one long ripping tear of canvas, and the Allies called it Hitler's buzzsaw. The US Army literally produced training films just to calm soldiers who froze up at the sound. Same cartridge from a quiet infantry rifle all the way up to that buzz saw. Germany's pistol round was the 9 by19 Parabellum feeding the Luger, the P38, and the MP40 submachine gun. reliable, compact, efficient, and today it's the single most popular pistol and submachine gun cartridge on Earth, sitting in police holsters on every continent. It was built for Hitler's army, and it outlived that army by generations. But the real prize is a stubby little thing most people have never heard of. By 1943, German designers noticed something almost no one else had acted on. Soldiers hardly ever fought at the extreme ranges their big full power rifle rounds were designed for. Most firefights happened close and fast. So they shortened the round creating the 7.9 2x33 Kurs Kurs meaning short. They chambered it in the STG44, the Sturm Gu, the first true assault rifle in history. Select fire controllable, a 30 round magazine, murderous at the ranges that actually mattered. Legend has it Hitler himself coined the dramatic name Sturmg Storm Rifle for its propaganda punch and it was the blueprint for everything that came after. Look at the AK-47, the M16, the rifle in every modern war on the news. Every single one is a grandchild of the idea Germany loaded into that short cartridge in 1943. A middle round halfway between a pistol and a full rifle that let one man carry the firepower of a small squad. The right collapsed in 1945. The concept it invented is still being fired in every war on Earth right now. Six nations, dozens of cartridges. A war we remember for its steel monsters, but one that was also fought and often decided by the little brass rounds a single soldier could hold in one hand. Some were pathetic, some were nearly invisible. Some were designed to kill a man and ended up killing an Empire's supply chain instead. And a handful, the Soviet 7.62x 62x 54R, the American 50BMG, that short German assault rifle round, are still being fired in wars happening today, long after the empires that forged them crumbled into dust. That's the eerie truth about ammunition. The tank rusts, the battleship sinks, the empire falls, but the bullet just gets handed to the next war.
